newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar dives on eve of Fed policy meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dollar dives on eve of Fed policy meeting.

text.p: The dollar dived against the yen ahead of a meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting body on Tuesday as traders faced up the consequences of a turnabout in Washington's commitment to a strong U.S. currency.
Panic selling pushed the dollar briefly below 113 yen in the afternoon from a high of 115.67 yen earlier in the day.
The greenback has been spiralling downward ever since hitting a 56-month peak of 127.47 yen on May 1.
Traders cited comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin as evidence of Washington's change in tune.
Rubin, speaking in Washington, said the U.S. policy on the dollar remained unchanged -- but did not explicitly repeat his past support for a strong dollar.

"People knew that Washington has been wanting a weak dollar against the yen in light of Japan's mushrooming surplus, but they had been unable to face up to the fact," said a chief trader at a major U.S. bank.

That reluctance to see the shift in the U.S. stance was partly because many had overbought the dollar over the past several months and partly because Rubin's turn of phrase has been very subtle, perhaps intentionally, the trader added.

"The dollar's nosedive (on Tuesday) was due to panic selling by those people who have simply bought too much since January for no good reason," said Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's international treasury department.

Traders said Washington had already hinted at its shift in stance, but had shied away from explicit endorsement of a strong yen for fear of causing the dollar to fall against other currencies as well. That is because a strong dollar has not only helped hold down U.S. inflation and interest rates but also attracted vital foreign investment.
Japanese policy-makers, meanwhile, have added to market confusion and delayed dollar selling by trying to put the brakes on a further dollar decline.

The dollar was also battered on Tuesday by expectations of a shrinking interest rate gap between the United States and Japan and worries that a sharp rise in Japan's trade surplus will spark friction with Washington.
Many market players expect the U.S. Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged at its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting later in the day.

Domestic media, meanwhile, reported that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) would recommend later this month that Japan raise its official discount rate from its current record low 0.5 percent to keep capital from flowing out of the country following liberalisation of foreign exchange laws.
An LDP source said later that there had been no decision yet on whether to recommend raising the key rate, but added that there were calls in the party to do so.

Fresh worries about Japan's rising trade surplus, a key component of its broader current account, also boosted the yen against the dollar after Rubin again warned against a sustained increase in Japan's current account surplus.
"The question is will there be a sustained increase in the current account surplus? And if so I think that is a very serious problem," he said.

Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus grew 163.7 percent to 831.48 billion yen ($7.35 billion) in April and its trade gap with the United States soared 174.1 percent to 468.97 billion yen ($4.15 billion).

Analysts said the only quick option now available for Japan to avoid a swelling external surplus was to strengthen the yen. Another option for Japan is drastic deregulation of its economy to create domestic demand for growth. But they said this would take too long to bring about, leaving a stronger yen as the only option for Japan to rein in its surplus. ($1=113 yen)
